**Clayton, Dubilier and Rice targets buyout of $40bn payments processor Global Payments**

*A potential take-private of one of the world's largest merchant acquirers would be the biggest payments leveraged buyout on record, reshaping competitive dynamics in merchant acquiring and pressuring rivals such as Fiserv and Adyen.*

Clayton, Dubilier and Rice is pursuing a buyout of Global Payments, the US-based payments processor with an enterprise value of approximately $40 billion, according to the Financial Times. A deal of that scale would dwarf previous private equity transactions in the payments industry and signal renewed appetite for large-cap targets after a period of subdued dealmaking.

Global Payments operates merchant acquiring, issuer processing and business software across more than 170 countries. The company has been reshaping its portfolio, having agreed in 2025 to sell its issuer solutions business to Fidelity National Information Services and completed its acquisition of Worldpay on January 9, 2026. A take-private would remove the company from public market scrutiny during what could be an extended period of integration and restructuring.

The deal comes amid a broader pattern of private equity interest in payments infrastructure. Pollen Street's carve-out of Finastra's Universal Banking business, Ingenico's recapitalisation with Pimco-led investors and the Stripe-Advent approach for PayPal all point to a conviction among financial sponsors that payments assets remain undervalued relative to their recurring revenue profiles. Whether CD&R can finance a transaction of this magnitude in the current rate environment remains the central question.

*Sources: [PE firm CD&R targets buyout of $40bn Global Payments - FT](https://www.finextra.com/newsarticle/48681/pe-firm-cdr-targets-buyout-of-40bn-global-payments---ft?utm_medium=rssfinextra&utm_source=finextrafeed) — Finextra*

**ECB selects network service providers for digital euro platform**

*Two providers have been chosen to build the connectivity layer linking payment service providers and national central banks to the digital euro service platform, moving the project from design into infrastructure procurement.*

The digital euro is moving from policy design into infrastructure build. The European Central Bank has selected two network service providers to handle connectivity between payment service providers, national central banks and the digital euro service platform. The selection follows the ECB's appointment of 36 payment providers for the digital euro pilot phase in July and advances the project into the procurement of core technical infrastructure.

The network layer is a critical component: it determines how transactions flow between end users' banks and the central settlement system. The decision to appoint dedicated providers rather than rely on existing interbank messaging infrastructure means the ECB is building a purpose-built stack, consistent with its stated goal of ensuring the digital euro operates as a distinct payment rail rather than an overlay on existing schemes.

The European Parliament voted on July 9 to open negotiations on the digital euro regulation. With both the legislative and technical workstreams progressing in parallel, the procurement decisions made now will shape the cost structure and technical constraints that banks and payment firms face when the system reaches production. Providers not selected at this stage may find it harder to influence the platform's architecture later.

*Sources: [ECB picks digital euro network service providers](https://www.finextra.com/newsarticle/48678/ecb-picks-digital-euro-network-service-providers?utm_medium=rssfinextra&utm_source=finextrafeed) — Finextra*

**Albania prepares to go live on TIPS-based instant payments in November**

*The launch would make Albania one of the first Western Balkan states to connect to European instant payment infrastructure, extending the reach of the Trans-European Instant Payment System settlement model beyond the EU.*

Albania is expected to launch a new instant payments system based on the Trans-European Instant Payment System (TIPS) model in November, according to The Banker. The system would enable real-time retail payments within the country and, in time, could provide a pathway toward cross-border interoperability with euro area instant payment schemes.

The move fits a broader pattern of EU candidate and neighbouring states adopting European payment standards ahead of accession. Montenegro launched instant payments using a TIPS Clone model in July, and Italy is completing a project to connect Balkan payment systems with EU infrastructure. For these countries, alignment with TIPS reduces the cost and complexity of future integration with the single euro payments area.

Albania's banking sector has been accelerating its digital transformation, and instant payments provide a foundation for further developments including mobile wallets, bill payments and merchant acceptance. The choice of TIPS rather than a proprietary domestic system reflects the gravitational pull of the EU's payment infrastructure standards on neighbouring economies.

*Sources: [Albania's banks accelerate digital transformation](https://www.thebanker.com/content/bdc26797-9c9b-41be-af27-427c29f614a9) — The Banker*

**Gambling Commission uses open banking to map black market betting harm**

*The first open banking study of unlicensed gambling sites finds that 91% of repeat users also bet with licensed operators, challenging assumptions behind the Gambling Commission's planned financial risk assessments that focus solely on licensed platforms.*

The UK Gambling Commission has published its first study using open banking data to examine the relationship between unlicensed gambling sites and licensed operators. The findings show that 91% of consumers who repeatedly transacted with illegal sites also held accounts with licensed operators, and that this cohort exhibited a heavy concentration of gambling harm indicators.

The study's implications cut in two directions. For proponents of open banking-based affordability checks, it validates the technology's capacity to surface patterns of harm across a consumer's full financial picture. But the finding that nearly all black market users also gamble with licensed operators complicates the argument that tighter affordability checks on licensed sites will simply push consumers toward unregulated alternatives. The data suggests the two markets overlap almost entirely rather than acting as substitutes.

The Gambling Commission confirmed in July that financial risk assessments using open banking would form part of its regulatory approach. This study provides the first empirical basis for understanding how those assessments might capture harm that spans both licensed and unlicensed activity, a gap that purely account-level monitoring cannot close.

*Sources: [Gambling Commission payment data: 91% of repeat illegal-site users still bet with licensed sites](https://casinobeats.com/2026/11/01/gambling-commission-payment-data-91-of-repeat-illegal-site-users-still-bet-with-licensed-sites/) — Casinobeats*
